Gambling Tax Basics: How Winnings and Losses Are Reported

Published October 8, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Every regulated sportsbook and casino in the US hands the IRS a copy of your homework whether you ask for one or not. Not every winning bet gets reported individually — a $20 same-game parlay that cashes for $140 almost never generates a form — but enough of them do that most active bettors eventually see at least one show up in their account documents. This guide covers how gambling winnings and losses are generally reported in the US, when an operator is actually required to tell the IRS about a specific payout, and a federal change that took effect for the 2026 tax year that quietly reduced how much of a losing bettor's losses they can write off. None of this is tax advice — gambling tax questions get complicated fast depending on your state, your filing status, and how much you play, and a preparer who has handled a few of these returns before is worth the fee.

  2. Form W-2G: when a win gets reported automatically

The basic rule: all winnings count as income

The IRS treats gambling winnings as taxable "other income," full stop. It doesn't matter whether the payout came from a $5 parlay or a six-figure poker score, whether you received any paperwork for it, or whether you ultimately lost more than you won across the rest of the year — each individual win is income in the year you received it. It also doesn't matter whether the sportsbook you used happened to be licensed in your state; the tax code doesn't carve out an exception for winnings from an unlicensed or offshore account, it just taxes the income regardless of where it came from. Withdrawable site credit, converted bonus bets, and free-bet payouts that you cash out all count the same way once they become money you can actually access.

Form W-2G: when a win gets reported automatically

A W-2G is the form an operator sends both to you and to the IRS when a specific win crosses a reporting threshold that's set by category of game, not by a single universal dollar amount. The thresholds that show up most often:

Game typeW-2G threshold
Slot machine (single jackpot)$1,200 or more
Bingo$1,200 or more
Keno$1,500 or more (net of the wager)
Poker tournament$5,000 or more (net of buy-in)
Sports betting & pari-mutuel pools$600 or more, and the payout is at least 300 times the wager

The "300-to-1" rule is the one that trips up sports bettors the most. A standard -110 spread or moneyline bet almost never pays anywhere near 300 times the stake, so most single wagers — even large ones — never generate a W-2G at all. A long-shot parlay or a futures bet is a different story: a $20 preseason divisional-winner future at +3000 pays exactly $600, which is 300 times the stake and crosses both thresholds, triggering a W-2G. A $5 ticket on a longer shot at +12000 pays $600 at 1,200 times the stake and triggers one just as easily, even though the dollar amount is identical to the first example.

Important: not receiving a W-2G does not mean a win is tax-free. It only means the operator's automatic reporting obligation didn't kick in — you're still legally required to report the income yourself.

Separately from the W-2G reporting threshold, there's a higher bar for mandatory federal withholding on certain pooled wagers (sports pools, lotteries, and similar pari-mutuel-style payouts): once net winnings exceed $5,000 and are still at least 300 times the wager, the payer is generally required to withhold 24% of the win up front, the same way a paycheck withholds income tax. That withheld amount shows up on the W-2G and gets credited against whatever you owe when you file.

Reporting without a W-2G: the session approach

Most of what a typical bettor wins never touches a W-2G, which raises the practical question of how it's supposed to be reported at all. The IRS has acknowledged, in limited guidance aimed mainly at slot play, that winnings and losses from a single continuous session at one establishment can be netted together rather than tracked bet by bet — win $300 across an afternoon of play, lose $220 of it back before you leave, and the session nets to an $80 gain for reporting purposes. Formal guidance on applying that same session concept to sports betting is thinner, since the tax code generally treats each wager as its own separate transaction. In practice, many bettors lean on the annual win/loss activity statement most licensed operators will generate on request, use it to total up the year's net results, and report the winning side as income on Schedule 1. Treat that as a starting point rather than the final word, particularly if you bet across several operators or states in the same year.

Deducting losses — and the 2026 cap that caught bettors off guard

For years, a bettor who itemized deductions on Schedule A could write off gambling losses dollar-for-dollar against gambling winnings — not against other income, and never below zero, but a full offset up to the amount won. Starting with the 2026 tax year, a federal law change limits that deduction to 90% of losses, still capped at the amount of winnings. The gap that creates is what the industry has taken to calling "phantom income": a bettor who wins $50,000 and loses $50,000 over the year — a net wash in their actual bank account — can now only deduct $45,000 of those losses, leaving $5,000 of winnings taxed with no offsetting write-off, even though they didn't come out ahead by a single dollar.

This cap only affects people who itemize. If you take the standard deduction instead, the older rule already meant zero loss deduction of any kind — you'd report 100% of your winnings as income with no offset at all, a bigger practical hit for most casual bettors than the new 90% cap is for high-volume ones.

The change has drawn real pushback from both the gambling industry and professional gamblers, and there's active legislation aimed at restoring the full 100% deduction — see our coverage of the House committee bill working through Congress for where that effort currently stands. As of this writing, the 90% cap remains current law, so it's worth confirming the status before you file rather than assuming either version applies.

The records that actually matter

Four things cover most of what you'd want on hand if a return ever gets a second look: the annual win/loss statement from each operator you used (available from account settings or by request, though these can undercount or miscategorize bonus-bet activity, so treat them as a starting point rather than gospel); a personal log of significant wagers with the date, the bet, the amount risked, and the result; bank or card statements showing deposits into and withdrawals from betting accounts; and copies of any W-2G forms you actually received. None of this needs to be elaborate — a simple spreadsheet updated weekly beats trying to reconstruct a year of activity from memory in April.

Mistakes that show up at tax time

The same handful of mistakes come up repeatedly. The biggest is assuming that no W-2G means no obligation — plenty of profitable bettors go a full year without ever seeing one and still owe tax on the total. Close behind it is forgetting that bonus bets and profit-boost winnings count the same as cash once they're withdrawable, not just the money that came directly from a card deposit. A third is not itemizing at all and losing out on any loss deduction whatsoever, which for a recreational bettor who had one big win and a lot of smaller losses can be a far larger tax bill than expected. And daily fantasy sports entries sometimes get lumped in with sports betting activity when they're actually reported under a different set of forms (commonly a 1099-MISC or 1099-K depending on the platform and amount) — worth separating out rather than guessing.

Everything above describes general federal rules as they commonly apply — it isn't personalized tax advice, and state-level treatment of gambling winnings and losses varies widely, with some states disallowing a loss deduction entirely even when you itemize on your federal return. Talk to a tax professional about your specific situation, especially in a year with a large win.

For the betting side of the ledger rather than the tax side, our bankroll management guide covers how to think about staking before the money ever reaches a tax form.

Frequently asked questions

Do I owe tax on a win if I never received a W-2G for it?

Yes. The W-2G threshold only controls when the operator is required to report the win automatically — your own obligation to report all gambling income exists regardless of whether a form was issued.

Can I deduct my losses if I take the standard deduction?

No. Gambling losses are only deductible if you itemize on Schedule A, and even then the deduction is now capped at 90% of your losses (up to the amount of your winnings) starting with the 2026 tax year.

Does a sportsbook automatically withhold taxes from a big win?

Only above a higher threshold than the W-2G reporting trigger — generally when net winnings exceed $5,000 and are at least 300 times the wager, which requires 24% federal withholding up front. Smaller wins that still generate a W-2G typically aren't withheld automatically.

Do states tax gambling winnings the same way the IRS does?

Most states with an income tax also tax gambling winnings, but the details vary significantly — some mirror federal rules closely, and others don't allow any loss deduction at all even if you itemize on your federal return. Check your specific state's treatment rather than assuming it matches federal rules.
